```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r model-load, include = FALSE}
mod <- readModelDb("Kinsale_2024_islatravir_rat")
ui <- rxode2::rxode(mod)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r ui$reference`
* Description: `r ui$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics16020201>
* Supplement (Table S1, PopPK model development; Figure S1, SAS release-model
  code): <https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/pharmaceutics16020201/s1>

Islatravir (ISL) is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase translocation inhibitor
under investigation for long-acting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).
Kinsale and colleagues gave single subcutaneous (SC) bolus doses of ISL to
Wistar rats and fitted a naive-pooled two-compartment model with first-order
absorption to the plasma ISL concentrations. They then divided the fitted
macro-constants by the mean administered dose to obtain ISL's unit impulse
response (UIR) in rats. They used that UIR to deconvolve the in vivo
absorption rate from published plasma PK of a reservoir-style
poly(caprolactone) ISL implant. The packaged model is the SC bolus PK model,
written in dose-proportional form so that its impulse response is exactly the
paper's UIR.

# Population

Seventy-two adult female Wistar rats (mean +/- SD body weight 0.307 +/-
0.02 kg) received a single SC bolus of 0.1, 0.3 or 1 mg/kg ISL under the neck
skin, 24 rats per dose level (Kinsale 2024 Section 2.2). The design was sparse
and destructive: three rats were sampled at each of 0.17, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6 and
24 h, one plasma sample per animal (Section 2.3). Of the plasma samples, 57 were
quantifiable; 6 were below the limit of quantification and 1 Grubbs outlier was
excluded (Section 3.1). The mean dose over all animals was 145,803 ng (Section
2.6).

```{r population}
str(ui$population)
```

# Source trace

Every `ini()` entry carries an in-file comment naming its origin in
`inst/modeldb/specificDrugs/Kinsale_2024_islatravir_rat.R`. They are collected
here for review.

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| `lka` (SC absorption rate constant) | 12.23 1/h | Supplementary Table S1, 'Final' column, `Ka (1/h)` (Figure 2 inset: 12) |
| `lalpha` (distribution-phase rate constant) | 1.21 1/h | Supplementary Table S1, 'Final', `alpha (1/h)`; Figure 2 inset; Section 3.2 (alpha1 = 1.2) |
| `lbeta` (terminal-phase rate constant) | 0.103 1/h | Supplementary Table S1, 'Final', `beta (1/h)`; Figure 2 inset; Section 3.2 (alpha2 = 0.103) |
| `lvc` (central volume) | 1.01967 L | Derived: Dref / (A + B), with Dref = 145,803 ng (Section 2.6) and A = 141.60, B = 1.39 ng/mL (Table S1, 'Final') |
| `lk21` (peripheral-to-central rate constant) | 0.11376 1/h | Derived: (A beta + B alpha) / (A + B), same Table S1 values |
| `propSd` | 0.76 | Section 3.2 ('76% residual error'); Table S1 model 6, RSE column 0.76 |
| No IIV | n/a | Section 2.6 ('naive pooled algorithm') |
| Two-compartment, first-order absorption, linear elimination | n/a | Section 2.6; Section 3.2; Supplementary Table S1 legend |
| `kel <- alpha * beta / k21`, `k12 <- alpha + beta - k21 - kel` | n/a | Standard two-compartment macro-to-micro identities |
| UIR = macro-constant / mean dose | n/a | Section 2.6 ('divided by the average dose (145,803 ng)') |
| Dosing: 0.1, 0.3, 1 mg/kg SC bolus | n/a | Section 2.2 |
| Implant mean absorption rate 0.072 (0.084 ISL-only, 0.061 ISL-plus) mg/day | n/a | Section 3.3 (used only in the illustration below) |

## The paper's unit impulse response

The fitted macro-constants describe the pooled data as one curve. Section 2.6
divides them by the mean dose, Dref = 145,803 ng, to obtain the UIR. The model
encodes that UIR through `vc` and `k21`, and its own impulse response can be
read back from the micro-constants and compared with the paper's numbers.

```{r uir}
p <- rxode2::rxSolve(
  mod,
  rxode2::et(amt = 1, cmt = "central") |> rxode2::et(0, cmt = "central")
) |>
  as.data.frame()

d_ref_ng <- 145803 # Section 2.6
a_fit <- 141.60 # Table S1 'Final' A (ng/mL)
b_fit <- 1.39 # Table S1 'Final' B (ng/mL)

# Impulse response of a two-compartment system in its macro form:
# coefficient_i = (k21 - lambda_i) / (vc * (lambda_j - lambda_i)), in 1/L.
uir_a1 <- (p$k21[1] - p$alpha[1]) / (p$vc[1] * (p$beta[1] - p$alpha[1]))
uir_a2 <- (p$k21[1] - p$beta[1]) / (p$vc[1] * (p$alpha[1] - p$beta[1]))
# 1/L is (mg/L) per mg dose = (1000 ng/mL) per (1e6 ng) = 1e-3 (ng/mL) per ng.
uir_a1_ng <- uir_a1 / 1000
uir_a2_ng <- uir_a2 / 1000

uir_tab <- tibble::tibble(
  Quantity = c("A1 (ng/mL per ng)", "A2 (ng/mL per ng)", "alpha (1/h)",
               "beta (1/h)"),
  Model = c(uir_a1_ng, uir_a2_ng, p$alpha[1], p$beta[1]),
  `Table S1 / Dref` = c(a_fit / d_ref_ng, b_fit / d_ref_ng, 1.21, 0.103),
  `Section 3.2 (printed)` = c(9.8e-4, 9.6e-6, 1.2, 0.103)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-Quantity, ~ formatC(.x, format = "g", digits = 4)))
knitr::kable(uir_tab, caption = "Unit impulse response of plasma ISL.")

# The encoding is an identity: the model's impulse response reproduces the
# Table S1 macro-constants divided by Dref to numerical precision.
stopifnot(
  abs(uir_a1_ng / (a_fit / d_ref_ng) - 1) < 1e-4,
  abs(uir_a2_ng / (b_fit / d_ref_ng) - 1) < 1e-4
)

derived <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("kel (1/h)", "k12 (1/h)", "CL (L/h)", "Q (L/h)", "Vp (L)",
                "Vss = Vc + Vp (L)", "t1/2 alpha (h)", "t1/2 beta (h)"),
  Value = c(p$kel[1], p$k12[1], p$cl[1], p$q[1], p$vp[1],
            p$vc[1] + p$vp[1], log(2) / p$alpha[1], log(2) / p$beta[1])
)
knitr::kable(derived, digits = 4,
             caption = "Clearance-parameterisation equivalents derived in model().")
```

Section 3.2 prints A1 = 9.8 x 10^-4^ ng/mL/ng, whereas 141.60 / 145,803 =
9.71 x 10^-4^ (and the rounded Figure 2 inset value, 142 / 145,803, gives
9.74 x 10^-4^). The printed A2 (9.6 x 10^-6^) is the rounded inset value
1.4 / 145,803. The model follows Table S1, the most precise source; the 1%
difference in A1 is below the reporting precision of the other parameters.

# Virtual cohort

The fit is naive pooled, so the model has no between-animal variability and
the simulations below are typical-value predictions. Each dose level is
represented by one rat of the mean body weight, 0.307 kg, sampled on the
paper's grid (0.17, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h) and on a dense grid for plotting.
A fourth subject receives the mean dose Dref = 145,803 ng, at which the model
reproduces the single fitted curve of Figure 2.

```{r cohort}
wt_kg <- 0.307 # Section 2.2 mean body weight
paper_grid <- c(0.17, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 24) # Section 2.3
dense_grid <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 25, by = 0.05), paper_grid)))

groups <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:4,
  treatment = c("0.1 mg/kg", "0.3 mg/kg", "1 mg/kg", "Dref (145,803 ng)"),
  amt = c(0.1 * wt_kg, 0.3 * wt_kg, 1 * wt_kg, d_ref_ng / 1e6)
)

make_events <- function(id, amt, treatment) {
  ev <- rxode2::et(amt = amt, cmt = "depot") |>
    rxode2::et(dense_grid, cmt = "central") |>
    as.data.frame()
  ev$id <- id
  ev$treatment <- treatment
  ev
}

events <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(groups)), function(i) {
  make_events(groups$id[i], groups$amt[i], groups$treatment[i])
}))

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(events[, c("id", "time", "evid")]),
  sum(events$evid == 1) == 4L
)
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = "treatment") |>
  as.data.frame()
stopifnot(identical(sort(unique(sim$id)), 1:4))
```

The model has no random effects, so the solve is deterministic; rxode2 notes
that the simulation has no `omega`.

# Replicate published figures

```{r figure-2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
# Replicates Figure 2 of Kinsale 2024: the single naive-pooled prediction of
# plasma ISL (ng/mL) for the three SC bolus doses, here the mean-dose subject,
# with the typical-value profiles of the three dose levels for context.
ggplot2::ggplot(
  dplyr::filter(sim, Cc > 0),
  ggplot2::aes(time, Cc, colour = treatment, linewidth = treatment)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c("0.1 mg/kg" = 0.5, "0.3 mg/kg" = 0.5, "1 mg/kg" = 0.5,
               "Dref (145,803 ng)" = 1.2)
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10(limits = c(0.01, 1000)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Time (h)", y = "Islatravir plasma concentration (ng/mL)",
    colour = NULL, linewidth = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure 2 of Kinsale 2024 (thick line = mean-dose prediction)."
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Figure 2's predicted curve is near 100 ng/mL at the first sample, falls to
about 1 ng/mL at 6 h, and to about 0.1 ng/mL at 24 h. The mean-dose prediction
takes the values below.

```{r figure-2-values}
fig2 <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(treatment == "Dref (145,803 ng)", time %in% c(0.17, 1, 6, 24)) |>
  dplyr::select(time, Cc)
knitr::kable(fig2, digits = 3,
             caption = "Mean-dose prediction at selected times (Figure 2 curve).")

# Figure 2 read on its log axis: about 0.8-0.9 ng/mL at 6 h and 0.1 ng/mL at 24 h.
c6 <- fig2$Cc[fig2$time == 6]
c24 <- fig2$Cc[fig2$time == 24]
stopifnot(c6 > 0.6, c6 < 1.2, c24 > 0.07, c24 < 0.15)
```

# PKNCA validation

Kinsale 2024 computed a sparse (naive-pooled) NCA per dose level with the
linear-up / log-down trapezoidal rule on the 0.17-24 h grid (Section 2.5). The
typical-value profiles are therefore evaluated on that same grid. At 0.1 mg/kg
the 24 h samples were not quantifiable (Section 3.1), so the 24 h point is
dropped for that dose and its `AUClast` ends at 6 h, as in the paper.

```{r pknca}
# The paper's sampling times plus the pre-dose time zero (pre-dose samples
# were all BLQ, Section 2.3; the simulated Cc at time zero is 0).
nca_times <- c(0, paper_grid)
sim_nca <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    treatment != "Dref (145,803 ng)",
    time %in% nca_times,
    !(treatment == "0.1 mg/kg" & time == 24)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, treatment) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time)
stopifnot(
  nrow(sim_nca) == 3L * length(nca_times) - 1L,
  all(sim_nca$Cc[sim_nca$time == 0] == 0)
)

dose_df <- groups |>
  dplyr::filter(treatment != "Dref (145,803 ng)") |>
  dplyr::mutate(time = 0)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(sim_nca, Cc ~ time | treatment + id,
                             concu = "ng/mL", timeu = "h")
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id, doseu = "mg")
intervals <- data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE,
                        auclast = TRUE)

nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(
  PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals,
                   options = list(auc.method = "lin up/log down"))
)
```

## Comparison against published NCA

Published values are from Kinsale 2024 Section 3.1 (plasma ISL; `Tmax` 10 min
at 0.1 and 1 mg/kg and 30 min at 0.3 mg/kg).

```{r nca-compare}
published <- tibble::tribble(
  ~treatment, ~cmax, ~tmax, ~auclast,
  "0.1 mg/kg", 22.6, 0.17, 16.2,
  "0.3 mg/kg", 44.7, 0.5, 54.8,
  "1 mg/kg", 201.3, 0.17, 229.6
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca_res,
  reference = published,
  by = "treatment",
  units = c(cmax = "ng/mL", tmax = "h", auclast = "h*ng/mL"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(
  cmp,
  caption = paste(
    "Typical-value NCA vs. published sparse NCA (Kinsale 2024 Section 3.1).",
    "* differs from reference by >20%."
  )
)
```

```{r nca-check}
sim_wide <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    dplyr::rename(published, cmax_pub = cmax, auclast_pub = auclast),
    by = "treatment"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cmax_ratio = cmax / cmax_pub,
    auclast_ratio = auclast / auclast_pub
  )

knitr::kable(
  sim_wide |>
    dplyr::select(treatment, cmax_ratio, auclast_ratio) |>
    dplyr::rename(
      "Dose level" = treatment,
      "Cmax ratio (model / published)" = cmax_ratio,
      "AUClast ratio (model / published)" = auclast_ratio
    ),
  digits = 2
)

# The model is dose proportional; the published AUClast rises more than
# proportionally (slope 1.15). The model sits at the high end at 0.1 mg/kg and
# closest at 1 mg/kg. Every ratio stays within a factor of two of the paper.
stopifnot(
  all(sim_wide$cmax_ratio > 0.5 & sim_wide$cmax_ratio < 2),
  all(sim_wide$auclast_ratio > 0.5 & sim_wide$auclast_ratio < 2)
)
```

At 1 mg/kg the typical-value `Cmax` and `AUClast` are within 20% of the
published values, and the low-dose `Cmax` agrees closely. Two discrepancies
exceed 20%, and both come from the published model and data rather than from
transcription:

* **`AUClast` at 0.1 and 0.3 mg/kg is overpredicted.** The pooled fit produced
  one curve for all three doses, and scaling that curve by dose / Dref is the
  paper's own UIR assumption (Section 2.6). The observed `AUClast`, however,
  rose more than proportionally with dose (log-log slope 1.15, Section 3.1).
  A dose-proportional model anchored near the mean dose therefore overpredicts
  the lower doses. The authors note that their diagnostics give the "best
  prediction for doses 0.3 mg/kg and higher", and that low-dose concentrations
  near the limit of quantification inflated the residual error.
* **`Cmax` and `Tmax` at 0.3 mg/kg.** The observed mid-dose peak fell at
  30 min, against 10 min for the other two doses. The authors attribute this
  to "random variability due to sparse sampling methods" with three
  destructively sampled rats per time point (Discussion). The typical-value
  model, with Ka = 12.23 1/h, peaks before 30 min at every dose.

# Implant illustration: zero-order systemic input

Section 3.3 reports a deconvolved mean in vivo absorption rate of
0.072 +/- 0.024 mg/day (ISL-only 0.084, ISL-plus 0.061 mg/day) for the
reservoir-style implant over 0-154 days, and Table 1 shows that a zero-order
model describes the cumulative absorbed mass well (mean r^2^ 0.946). The
deconvolution used the UIR as the systemic disposition, so the implant input
enters `central` directly. The illustration below applies these mean rates as
constant-rate inputs. It is not a fit to the implant data (the individual
implant PK was published separately and is not reproduced here). At steady
state the plasma concentration is rate / CL.

```{r implant, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
rates <- tibble::tibble(
  id = 1:3,
  treatment = c("Overall mean 0.072 mg/day", "ISL-only 0.084 mg/day",
                "ISL-plus 0.061 mg/day"),
  rate_mg_day = c(0.072, 0.084, 0.061)
)
t_end_h <- 154 * 24

ev_implant <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(rates)), function(i) {
  ev <- rxode2::et(
    amt = rates$rate_mg_day[i] * 154, rate = rates$rate_mg_day[i] / 24,
    cmt = "central"
  ) |>
    rxode2::et(seq(0, t_end_h, by = 24), cmt = "central") |>
    as.data.frame()
  ev$id <- rates$id[i]
  ev$treatment <- rates$treatment[i]
  ev
}))

sim_implant <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = ev_implant, keep = "treatment") |>
  as.data.frame()

ggplot2::ggplot(sim_implant, ggplot2::aes(time / 24, Cc, colour = treatment)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Time after implantation (day)",
                y = "Islatravir plasma concentration (ng/mL)", colour = NULL,
                caption = "Illustration: constant-rate input at the Section 3.3 mean absorption rates.") +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")

css <- sim_implant |>
  dplyr::filter(time == 100 * 24) |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, Cc) |>
  dplyr::mutate(`Rate / CL (ng/mL)` = rates$rate_mg_day / 24 / p$cl[1] * 1000)
knitr::kable(css, digits = 3, caption = "Plateau concentration at day 100.")

# Analytic steady state of a linear model under constant input.
stopifnot(all(abs(css$Cc / css$`Rate / CL (ng/mL)` - 1) < 1e-3))
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Naive-pooled fit, dose-proportional encoding.** The published fit reports
  the macro-constants A and B in ng/mL for one pooled curve across all three
  doses (Figure 2). The model writes the paper's UIR (A / Dref, B / Dref, with
  Dref = 145,803 ng from Section 2.6) as `vc` and `k21`, so a dose of Dref
  reproduces the fitted curve and other doses scale proportionally. This is
  the assumption the paper itself makes when it uses the UIR for
  deconvolution, and it is supported by the dose-proportionality slopes in
  Section 3.1. `lvc` and `lk21` are therefore derived values; the source-trace
  table gives their derivation.
* **Macro-constant reading with first-order absorption.** The model treats A
  and B as coefficients of the impulse (bolus) response, with first-order
  absorption convolved into it. This is how Section 2.6 uses them (A / dose =
  UIR) and is consistent with the stripping-dose macro parameterisation of
  Phoenix NLME. If A and B were instead the coefficients of the extravascular
  curve itself, A would be about 10% smaller (factor (Ka - alpha) / Ka =
  0.90) and B about 1% smaller. The two readings cannot be distinguished at
  the resolution of Figure 2.
* **Final-model estimates.** Values come from the 'Final' column of
  Supplementary Table S1 (model 6, 'Base Model no Outlier'), which matches the
  rounded Figure 2 inset. Section 3.2 prints A1 = 9.8 x 10^-4^ ng/mL/ng; the
  Table S1 value gives 9.71 x 10^-4^ (see the UIR section).
* **Residual error.** The 76% residual error of the Phoenix multiplicative
  error model (Section 3.2; Table S1, model 6) is encoded as proportional
  error, `propSd = 0.76`.
* **No IIV.** The naive-pooled algorithm estimates no between-animal
  variability, so the model has no etas; this reflects the analysis design,
  not an unreported variance.
* **Body weight.** Doses are mg/kg. The vignette uses the mean body weight
  (0.307 kg) to convert to mg; the model has no weight covariate because the
  paper's fit has none.
* **Not modelled.** Intracellular ISL-triphosphate in PBMCs was analysed by NCA
  only. The deconvolution and the four release-kinetic regressions (Table 1)
  produce rates and goodness-of-fit statistics rather than model parameters
  (zero-order and Ritger-Peppas rate constants are not reported). The implant
  appears only as the constant-rate illustration above.
* **Errata.** A literature search on 2026-10-29 (Europe PMC) found no erratum
  or correction for this article.
